title: Naturalised species are usually not closely allied to the natives they join

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Naturalised species are usually not closely allied to the natives they join

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Species that become naturalised in new countries are generally not closely allied to the native inhabitants but are very distinct, often belonging to genera absent from the region, whereas closely allied species equally well fitted to their places tend to keep separate.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the forms which become naturalised in new countries are not generally closely allied to the aboriginal inhabitants, but are very distinct species, belonging in a large proportion of cases, as shown by Alph. de Candolle, to distinct genera.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XII, “Geographical Distribution, continued”; section “On the relation of the inhabitants of islands to those of the nearest mainland”. Scope: naturalised (introduced) plants and animals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch12-14: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.76

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Relatedness and establishment are measurable, and substantial open plant data exist. The comparison needed to infer that close relatives are equally fitted is poorly observed, so only the general pattern is currently resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare taxonomic and phylogenetic distance from established introduced species to recipient native floras and faunas against matched non-naturalized introductions or source pools. A predominance of distant naturalizers, including genera absent natively, supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Global naturalization data are much stronger for plants than animals.

Introduction effort and propagule pressure confound establishment.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Genus absence and phylogenetic distance to natives are measurable readings of 'not closely allied', and global naturalised-plant lists already tabulate the main botanical pattern Darwin cited. Animal coverage is thinner, but introduced-status occurrences are public and the same test applies. The analysis is standard and has been run before; transport bias and source-pool choice are the reasons discriminating power stays moderate.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For regional floras and faunas, compare the phylogenetic distance of naturalised species to the native biota, and the fraction whose genus is absent from the natives, against a null draw from the pool of species that could have been introduced. The claim is confirmed if successful naturalisations are concentrated in genera missing from the region, and refuted if they are as closely allied to natives as the introduction pool.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Animal naturalisation inventories are less complete and less standardised than the plant compilation.

Humans preferentially transport particular families, so an apparent excess of distinct genera can be an introduction bias.

The result depends on how the source pool is defined, including which species had the opportunity to be moved.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: In well-documented regional floras, vascular plant species naturalised in a region belong to genera that have no native species there more often than do the species that have naturalised elsewhere in the world but not in that region (the pool of proven colonists that could have joined it).

fields.label: Method
fields.value: WCVP accepted non-hybrid species and their non-doubtful level-3 distribution records were loaded. For each of the 24 pre-registered regions (all present, all with >= 457 naturalised species), the native genera were those with a native, non-extinct species in the region; the naturalised set was the species recorded as introduced and not native there; the pool was every species recorded as introduced in at least one other region and with no record in the region. The share of each set in genera without native species was compared by odds ratio and one-sided Fisher exact tests in both directions, and regions significant in each direction were counted against the two-thirds threshold.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: using WCVP (World Checklist of Vascular Plants, Kew) accepted non-hybrid species and their non-doubtful TDWG level-3 distribution records, for each of 24 fixed regions R: native genera G_R = genera with >= 1 species recorded native (introduced = 0, extinct = 0) in R; naturalised set N_R = species recorded introduced in R and not native in R; pool P_R = species recorded introduced in >= 1 other level-3 region and with no record (native or introduced) in R. 'Novel' = genus not in G_R. Odds ratio OR_R = odds(novel | N_R) / odds(novel | P_R), Fisher exact test one-sided in each direction. Regions with |N_R| < 50 are dropped. SUPPORTS if, among the remaining regions, at least two thirds have OR_R > 1 with one-sided p < 0.05 (naturalised species over-represented in genera absent from the native flora).

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: REFUTES if at least two thirds of the remaining regions have OR_R < 1 with one-sided p < 0.05 (naturalised species significantly more likely than the colonist pool to have native congeners). Any other outcome is MIXED. If fewer than 12 regions remain the result is inconclusive (underpowered); if WCVP cannot be downloaded, inconclusive (data-unavailable). The fraction of naturalised species in novel genera (Darwin's and de Candolle's 'large proportion ... distinct genera') is recorded per region as a descriptive statistic and does not enter the verdict.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: fraction of regions where naturalised plants are significantly MORE likely than the colonist pool to belong to genera already native (OR < 1, one-sided p < 0.05)

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: regions significant in Darwin's direction: 0/24; opposite direction: 23/24

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'not closely allied to the aboriginal inhabitants ... belonging in a large proportion of cases ... to distinct genera' is read at the genus level (the level de Candolle used): a naturalised species is 'closely allied' to the natives if its genus has a native species in the region. The claim is comparative in substance (closely allied species 'tend to keep separate'), so the test compares naturalised species with a colonist pool rather than with zero; the pool is all species proven able to naturalise somewhere, which controls for the fact that only some plants become weeds at all. WCVP 'introduced' records are taken as naturalised occurrences. Restricted to vascular plants, the group de Candolle and Darwin discussed; animals are out of scope of this test. The 24 regions are TDWG level-3 units with well-documented floras on every continent and oceanic islands: NZN, NZS, HAW, GRB, IRE, FRA, GER, SPA, ITA, CAL, TEX, FLA, NSW, VIC, WAU, TAS, CPP, CLC, AGE, JAP, MAU, REU, CNY, AZO; codes absent from WCVP are dropped and reported.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP), Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: wcvp_names.csv and wcvp_distribution.csv

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The comparative part of the claim is refuted: in 23 of 24 regions (all but north-eastern Argentina, which is not significant) naturalised species are significantly more likely than the pool of proven colonists to belong to a genus already native to the region (median odds ratio 0.60; in Great Britain 48% of naturalised species are in novel genera against 70% of the pool, in Germany 42% against 71%). No region shows Darwin's direction. This agrees with the modern literature on 'Darwin's naturalisation hypothesis', which usually finds naturalised plants closer to natives than expected.

The descriptive part that Darwin attributes to de Candolle holds: a median 56% of naturalised species per region belong to genera with no native species (40% in Japan to 77% on Hawaii), which is 'a large proportion of cases'. The verdict rests on the pre-registered comparative criterion, because only it tests 'not closely allied ... whereas closely allied species ... tend to keep separate'.

The colonist pool is not climate-matched: many pool species come from climates where a region's native genera are absent and could not naturalise there for climatic reasons, which inflates the pool's novelty and biases the test against Darwin. Humans also preferentially introduce plants from floras similar to the recipient region (e.g. European weeds to other temperate regions), which creates congener overlap independent of establishment success.

WCVP 'introduced' covers naturalised occurrences without separating casual from established populations; genus is a coarse measure of being 'closely allied' and genus concepts vary across families.

Plants only; Darwin's statement also covers animals.
